item.title: Google's four TPUs in one year: what 8tx and 8i Max mean for anyone negotiating with Nvidia
item.description: Confidential compute for fine-tuning and a doubled-up inference chip extend the eighth-generation line, and the software around it is now the real competitive move.
item.content:encoded:
Confidential compute for fine-tuning and a doubled-up inference chip extend the eighth-generation line, and the software around it is now the real competitive move.

Google announced two more eighth-generation TPU systems on November 9, bringing to four the number it has introduced this year, a cadence it says it has never managed before. TPU 8t for large-scale training and TPU 8i for real-time inference arrived at Cloud Next in April; TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max complete the set.

The two new systems

TPU 8tx uses the same silicon as 8t but pairs it with fifth-generation AMD EPYC host CPUs to deliver hardware-level confidential computing, keeping both data and model weights isolated while in use. Google positions it for secure inference and for small-scale training, fine-tuning, distillation and reinforcement learning on sensitive data that cannot leave a customer's trust boundary. It borrows the Boardfly interconnect from 8i and Google claims up to half the latency of 8t with a negligible performance penalty.

TPU 8i Max packages two 8i chips together, doubling compute, on-chip SRAM and HBM bandwidth per package while fitting into the existing rack footprint. It is aimed at very long context windows and at squeezing more compute out of each square foot and each watt, the two constraints that now bind data-centre operators more than chip supply does. Google gave no pricing or availability dates for either system.

The software is the story

The hardware announcements came wrapped in a software release that matters more for adoption. TorchTPU, open-sourced in October, lets PyTorch code and Hugging Face models run natively on TPUs, with backends for the vLLM and SGLang serving engines that most inference teams already use. An open-source XLA Serving Engine runs models across TPUs, GPUs and CPUs from one C++ runtime. TPU Sync tiers key-value caches across chip memory, host DRAM and storage, and Google claims it cuts cache transfer latency and time-to-first-token by more than 90%. Cloud Pathways and GKE dynamic slicing, which assemble and partition TPU topologies through optical circuit switching, are now generally available. There is even a preview TPU agent suite that plugs into Claude Code, Cursor and Antigravity to diagnose bottlenecks and autotune kernels.

For years the honest objection to TPUs was that the software assumed JAX and a Google-shaped workflow. That objection is now largely gone, which is why the claim of nearly 100 TPU customers, including frontier labs and trading firms, is more credible than it would have been in 2024.

Why Nvidia buyers should care

Nvidia's pricing power rests on CUDA lock-in and on the absence of a second supplier that can deliver training-class systems at scale. Four TPU systems in a year, with a PyTorch-native stack and confidential compute, is the most direct challenge to both. Buyers rarely need to move workloads to benefit: a credible alternative in the room changes the terms of a GPU reservation or a multi-year cloud commitment. It also arrives in a week when Nvidia's own governance is under an independent board review, which sharpens any procurement committee's interest in a second source.

The counter-argument

TPUs are only available through Google Cloud, so the choice is also a choice of cloud, and that lock-in is arguably tighter than CUDA's. Google's performance claims are its own and the two new systems have no public pricing. Most enterprise inference still runs on models whose vendors optimise first for Nvidia, and Anthropic's new Fable 5.2 fast mode, for example, is available on Google Cloud but was engineered on mixed hardware. The practical gap between 'runs on TPU' and 'runs best on TPU' is where migration projects stall.

What to do

Ask your Google account team for 8tx and 8i Max pricing and dates in writing. Run one production inference service through vLLM on TPU 8i and compare cost per million output tokens against your current GPU fleet. If you handle regulated data, request the confidential-compute attestation flow for 8tx and have your security team review it. And whatever the outcome, bring the numbers to your next Nvidia or cloud renewal.

item.title: Nvidia's board is investigating Jensen Huang. Here is what is actually at stake
item.description: An independent review, an admitted affair and a November 18 congressional briefing turn a personal scandal into a governance test for the company the whole AI stack depends on.
item.content:encoded:
An independent review, an admitted affair and a November 18 congressional briefing turn a personal scandal into a governance test for the company the whole AI stack depends on.

Nvidia's board of directors announced on Sunday, November 8, that its independent directors, working with outside legal counsel, will review CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at the Singapore-based chip company Megaspeed. The same day, Huang sent a message to employees acknowledging an affair with her, apologising to his family and colleagues and saying he had fallen short of his responsibility to the company.

The board's statement paired the review with two reassurances: it said it has "no reason to believe" national-security or company secrets were compromised, and that it has confidence in Huang and his leadership team. Huang said he supports the review and will cooperate.

How we got here

We covered the first chapter yesterday: a New York Times report that a memo circulated among US policymakers earlier this year alleged Alice Huang had been recruited by China's Ministry of State Security to gather information on Nvidia's chief executive. Nvidia's initial response was that the two executives' interactions were "not unusual" and that the company does not share classified information with customers. Megaspeed is a Nvidia customer, and the company has been a focus of earlier reporting on how advanced GPUs reach China despite US export controls.

What changed on Sunday is that the personal relationship is no longer in dispute, and the board has formally taken ownership of the question. House committee chairs had already requested a closed-door briefing from Huang, scheduled for November 18.

Why this is a governance story, not a gossip story

Nvidia is not a normal company. Its GPUs run the overwhelming majority of frontier AI training, its export licences are a lever of US foreign policy, and its chief executive is the single most influential individual in the AI supply chain. A founder-CEO in that position who was, on the available reporting, in a relationship with a suspected intelligence asset raises three distinct questions a board has to answer separately.

First, was anything disclosed that should not have been? The board says it has no reason to think so, but that is a starting position, not a finding. Second, did the relationship create leverage, regardless of whether anything was disclosed? Counter-intelligence professionals treat a secret affair as a classic coercion vector, which is why executive-protection programmes at defence contractors cover personal conduct. Third, does the episode change how Washington treats Nvidia's China business, which is already under scrutiny from both parties?

Yale's Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, who studies CEO succession, told TechCrunch he puts Huang's survival odds at roughly 50-50. That is a sharper read than the board's language, but it reflects a real pattern: boards that open independent reviews while expressing confidence usually mean it, and the outcome tends to turn on what the review finds rather than on the initial scandal.

The counter-argument

The case for calm is that Nvidia's commercial position does not depend on one person. Its software moat, supply agreements and customer relationships are institutional. A leadership transition at a $4-trillion-class company would be disruptive but survivable, and the stock has absorbed worse news in the past week, when the Nasdaq 100 shed a record $2.3 trillion and Nvidia alone lost around $450 billion in value on election and demand worries.

The case against calm is that Huang is unusually central to Nvidia's strategy, its China diplomacy and its customer relationships, and that this story has moved from a single-outlet report to a board action and an admission in nine days.

What to watch

The November 18 congressional briefing is the next hard date. Watch whether any part of it becomes public, whether the Commerce Department or BIS reference the episode in any export-licensing decision, and whether the board sets a timetable for the review. Also watch Megaspeed: any regulatory action against it would reopen the chip-diversion thread this story grew out of. We will update this article as the review progresses.

item.title: Ramp's data says business AI spending has flattened. Here is how to read it
item.description: A plateau in the share of companies paying for AI tools is not the end of adoption. It is the end of buying everything.
item.content:encoded:
A plateau in the share of companies paying for AI tools is not the end of adoption. It is the end of buying everything.

Ramp, the corporate card and bill-pay company, publishes an index built from what its customers actually pay for. TechCrunch reported on November 6 that the latest reading shows the share of US businesses paying for AI tools has flattened in recent months after two years of steady growth. The timing, days before Anthropic's IPO marketing begins, guaranteed attention.

What the data measures, and what it does not

Ramp's index measures breadth: the fraction of businesses with at least one AI subscription or usage charge. It is a good proxy for "has tried AI," and that number saturating was always going to happen; most companies that were going to buy a ChatGPT or Claude seat have done so.

It does not measure depth: how much each adopter spends, how many seats, how much API usage. Breadth can flatten while depth rises, which is the pattern in most enterprise software categories after the trial phase. It also undercounts spend that flows through cloud bills (Azure, AWS, Google Cloud), where most API usage is invoiced.

The pilot cull

What is almost certainly happening underneath is consolidation. Two years of experimentation produced, in many companies, five or six overlapping subscriptions and several pilots with no owner. Finance teams are now cancelling what did not produce measurable results and standardising on one or two platforms. That shows up as flat breadth and, often, higher spend per surviving vendor.

Why it matters for the IPO

Investors underwriting Anthropic, and OpenAI's next round, are paying for growth that depends on enterprise expansion. Flat adoption breadth is not fatal to that story, but it moves the burden of proof to depth: usage per customer, net revenue retention and API growth, numbers the S-1 and the roadshow will be pushed to disclose.

What to do with it

  • If you run a company: make the consolidation deliberate. List every AI line item, assign an owner and an outcome, and cancel the rest. The survivors will get better terms if you consolidate volume.
  • If you sell AI software: the land-grab phase is over. Expansion now comes from proving outcomes inside existing accounts, not from logos.
  • If you invest: ask every AI company for net revenue retention. It is the number this data makes unavoidable.
